0.note: **For the chief musician** is an instruction about who should lead people in singing or playing music with this psalm. This could refer to the person in charge of music for temple worship. If your readers would not be familiar with this role, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the worship leader]

1.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Praise**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [We are praising you in silence]

The implication is that the people are waiting silently in reverent worship before they praise God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Waiting in silence to praise] or [Silent before worship directed]
The word **Zion** is the name of a place. It refers to Mount Zion in Jerusalem.

The expression **a vow will be paid** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the worshipers. Alternate translation: [the worshipers will pay their vows] or [people will fulfill their vows]

2.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **prayer**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You who hear people when they pray;]

Here, **all flesh** represents all people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all people] or [everyone]

3.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The wrong things we have done]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ways we have disobeyed you]

The terms **iniquities** and **transgressions** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Our many sins overwhelm me but]

The pronoun **me** refers to the psalmist, while the pronoun “our” refers to the psalmist along with the rest of God’s people. The psalmist is speaking both personally and on behalf of the community. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [prevail against me and my people]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you cover them** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that God, to whom he is speaking, is the one forgiving them. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [you, God, you cover them]

The psalmist is using **you cover them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you forgive them” or “you atone for them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you forgive them] or [you atone for them]

4.note: The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is] or [Truly blessed is]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the good things in your house] or [how good your house is]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how holy your temple is]

Here, **your house** and **your temple** represent God’s presence at the temple in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your presence in the temple … your presence in the temple]

The terms **your house** and **your temple** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [May we be full of the goodness and holiness of your holy dwelling place]

5.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by doing what is right] or [in a righteous way]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who is saving us]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **confidence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the trusted one of]

The psalmist is using **the ends of the earth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the most distant places on earth” or “people everywhere.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the most remote places] or [people everywhere on earth]

The psalmist is referring to all of the earth by naming two extremes, **the ends of the earth** and **the distant seas**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everywhere on earth]

6.note: The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a builder who physically **establishes mountains** in place. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who created the mountains by his great power]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by how strong he is]

The expression **being girded with might** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [who girds himself with might] or [who clothes himself with might]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **might**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with powerful strength] or [by being mighty]

The terms **strength** and **might** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [great power]

The psalmist is speaking of might as if it were clothing that God could wear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [possessing great power] or [having great might]

7.note: These two phrases **the roar of the seas** and **the roar of their waves** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the roar of the seas, yes, the roar of their waves] or [the roaring seas and their waves]

The terms **the roar of the seas** and **the roar of their waves** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the loud roaring of the seas]

The psalmist is speaking of **the tumult of the peoples** as if it were roaring like chaotic seas. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the unrest of the nations] or [the agitation of the peoples]

The phrases **the roar of the seas** and **the tumult of the peoples** mean basically the same thing. The psalmist is speaking of the **peoples** as if they were **seas**, comparing the noise and chaos of nations to crashing waves. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the roar of the seas, that is, the tumult of the peoples]

8.note: The psalmist is using **the dwellers of the ends** as a common expression of the culture to mean “those who live in the farthest places” or “those who live at the remotest boundaries of the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who live in the most distant places] or [people in the remotest parts of the earth]

Here, **signs** represents God’s miraculous deeds. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your miraculous works] or [your mighty acts]

The psalmist is speaking of **the goings forth of the morning and the evening** as if they were living things that could **shout joyfully**. The phrase **the goings forth of the morning and the evening** represents sunrise and sunset. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the places where the sun rises and sets rejoice] or [people everywhere from sunrise to sunset shout joyfully]

The psalmist is using **the goings forth of the morning and the evening** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the east and the west” or “all the earth from sunrise to sunset.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all the earth from the east to the west] or [everywhere the sun rises and sets]

The psalmist is referring to all times of day by naming two extremes, **the morning** and **the evening**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all day long] or [at all times]

9.note: David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who could come to **visit the earth**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [You come to the earth and care for it] or [You attend to the earth]

The psalmist is speaking of the rain that comes from the sky as if it flowed from **the channel of God**, a heavenly waterway. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The sky is full of rain from God] or [God’s heavenly reservoir is full of water]

The pronoun **their** refers to people on earth who benefit from God’s provision. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [grain for people] or [grain for humanity]

10.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [You water its furrows, you settle its ridges]

The psalmist is speaking of the growth of plants as if it were something that receives God’s **blessing**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you cause its crops to grow] or [you make it produce a good harvest]

11.note: The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a king placing a **crown** on the year to adorn it with abundant blessings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You adorn the year with your goodness] or [You make the year wonderful with your goodness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how good you are] or [how generously you provide]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were driving a cart whose **tracks drip fatness** (that is, whose wheel ruts overflow with abundant crops). If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [you leave abundance behind you wherever you go]

Here, **tracks** represents God’s presence as he passes by, bringing blessing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everywhere you pass by] or [the places where you have gone]

Here, **fatness** represents abundance and prosperity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [abundance] or [rich blessings]

12.note: The psalmist is speaking of **the pastures of the wilderness** as if they were living things that could **drip** with moisture or abundance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The pastures of the wilderness are covered with dew] or [The pastures of the wilderness are full of water]

The psalmist is speaking of **the hills** as if they were living things that could put on clothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the hills are like people who dress themselves in joyful celebration] or [it is as if the hills wear rejoicing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rejoicing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [joy] or [what makes people rejoice]

The psalmist is speaking of the hills as if they were people who could **gird on rejoicing** like a person putting on clothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the hills are clothed with joy] or [the hills seem joyful]

13.note: The psalmist is speaking of **meadows** as if they were living things that could put on clothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Flocks cover the meadows]

The psalmist is speaking of the meadows as if they were people who could **put on** flocks as clothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The flocks cover the meadows] or [Flocks are spread across the meadows]

The psalmist is speaking of **the valleys** as if they were living things that could **cover themselves with grain**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [grain grows abundantly in the valleys] or [the valleys are filled with grain]

The psalmist is speaking of **the meadows** and **the valleys** as if they were living things that could **shout joyfully** and **sing**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It is as though they shout joyfully; indeed, it is as though they sing] or [They are like people shouting joyfully and singing]

The terms **shout joyfully** and **sing** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [rejoice with loud songs]
